common_name: Sarah Mountain Laurel (Vivid Red Bud and Flower Selection)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun. Sarah bears some of the reddest buds and flowers of any commonly grown mountain laurel cultivar.

directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Sarah bears vivid, saturated red buds that open to red-tinged flowers, among the deepest, most consistently red-toned mountain laurel cultivars available, standing out sharply from the more typical pink-and-white banded species flowers. It shares the species' gnarled, sculptural evergreen habit, making it a strong specimen or woodland-border shrub. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

common_name: Elf Mountain Laurel (Dwarf Pale Pink Compact Selection)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun. Elf is a true dwarf mountain laurel selection with pale pink buds opening to near-white flowers, well suited to small gardens.

directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Elf stays notably compact and dwarf for a mountain laurel, reaching only three to four feet at maturity with proportionally smaller leaves and flowers, bearing pale pink buds that open to near-white blooms. Its small stature makes it one of the few mountain laurel cultivars practical for a foundation planting or smaller garden bed. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

common_name: Peppermint Mountain Laurel (Bold Pink-and-White Candy-Striped Bands)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun. Peppermint bears bold, candy-striped pink-and-white flower bands, a bright, distinctive pattern among mountain laurel cultivars.

directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Peppermint bears bold, crisply defined candy-cane-striped bands of pink against white on each flower, a brighter, higher-contrast pattern than the softer pink-white banding typical of the species, opening on the classic gnarled, sculptural evergreen shrub. Its vivid, striking pattern makes it a strong specimen or woodland-border accent. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

common_name: Minuet Mountain Laurel (Dwarf White with Maroon Cinnamon Band)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun. Minuet is a dwarf mountain laurel selection with white flowers marked by a distinct maroon-cinnamon band inside each bloom.

directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Minuet stays compact and dwarf, well under the height of standard mountain laurel, bearing white flowers marked with a distinct maroon-cinnamon band ringing the inside of each bloom, a refined, jewel-like detail visible up close. Its small stature makes it a good fit for a foundation planting or smaller shaded garden bed. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

common_name: Bullseye Mountain Laurel (White Flowers with Bold Maroon Ring Pattern)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun. Bullseye bears white flowers marked with a bold, distinct maroon ring pattern, one of the most strikingly patterned mountain laurel cultivars.

directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Bullseye bears white flowers marked with a bold, wide maroon ring encircling the inner petal surface, an especially strong, graphic patterning that stands out even from a distance, opening on the classic gnarled, sculptural evergreen shrub habit typical of the species. Its striking pattern makes it a strong specimen or woodland-border accent. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.
